title: Talk to anyone
author: claude

topic.title: Talk to anyone
topic.description: Conversation skills from published studies. Most studies ran in the US or UK, often between strangers. The Indian scenes are for practice. The studies did not test them.

concepts.title: Follow-ups
concepts.hook: What can help a first chat move past small talk?
concepts.askLine: After someone tells you about their weekend, what could you ask next?
concepts.rule: Pick up what the person said and ask for more. A more personal question can take the chat one step deeper. Sharing back is a good habit, though the studies did not test it.

claims.text: People who ask more questions, mainly follow-up questions, are liked more.
A follow-up question asks the other person to say more about what they just said.
People do not expect this effect.
Chats with strangers felt less awkward and more connecting than people expected.
People most overrate the awkwardness of deep talk.
The reason: they expected partners to care less about what they shared than the partners really did.

misconceptions.name: A better story of my own shows interest.
misconceptions.correction: The studies measured questions, not stories. Asking about theirs went with being liked. Your story can come after.

misconceptions.name: Others won't care about deeper talk.
misconceptions.correction: In the studies, partners cared more than people expected.

sources.title: Huang et al. (2017), study of question asking
sources.publisher: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

sources.title: Kardas, Kumar and Epley (2022), study of deep conversations
sources.publisher: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

quest.title: Ask and share
quest.detail: With someone you already know, ask two follow-up questions and one deeper one. Share your own answer too. Skip any part that feels like too much.

steps.title: Ask one more question

hook.stem: In a first chat, who is usually liked more?

options.text: The one with the best stories.
options.feedback: The study points to asking more follow-up questions.

options.text: The one who asks more follow-up questions.
options.feedback: In studies, people who asked more follow-ups were liked more.

options.text: The one who talks about themselves the most.
options.feedback: The study did not test this. It found that people who asked more follow-ups were liked more by their partner.

steps.teach: Ask about the last thing they shared, so they can tell you are listening. In US first-chat studies, people who asked more follow-ups were liked more.

parts: Meera: "I went home to Nashik this weekend."
Arjun: "Nice, Nashik! I've never been."
Meera: "Helped my dad at his shop. Sale week."
Arjun: "What was the busiest part?"
Arjun: "My mama has a shop too. Diwali week is chaos."
example.feedback: Part 4 picks up 'shop' and 'sale week', so it is a follow-up. Part 5 shares something back. The authors guess that helps, but did not test it.

guided.stem: A classmate says: "Just got back from my cousin's wedding in Jaipur." Which reply is a follow-up?
guided.hint: Stay with what the classmate just said.

options.text: "How was it? Did anything funny happen?"
options.feedback: Right. It asks for more about the wedding they just mentioned.

options.text: "Cool. Did you finish the DBMS assignment?"
options.feedback: This changes the topic. A follow-up stays on what they said.

options.text: "Weddings are the best. Wait till you hear about my sister's sangeet..."
options.feedback: That is your story, not a question about theirs. The studies linked follow-up questions to being liked.

steps.takeaway: Ask about what they just said. Share your side after.

steps.title: Go one level deeper

hook.stem: Before a deep chat with someone new, most people guess it will feel...

options.text: More awkward than it turns out.
options.feedback: In studies, deep chats felt less awkward than people expected.

options.text: About as awkward as it turns out.
options.feedback: People in the studies expected more awkwardness than they felt.

options.text: Less awkward than it turns out.
options.feedback: The gap went the other way: the chats felt less awkward.

steps.teach: Deep talk may feel risky at first. Yet it can feel less odd than you fear, since the other person may care more than you think.

example.ask: Tap the first step past small talk.
parts: Small talk: "Which branch are you in?"
One step deeper: "Why did you pick it?"
Deeper: "What do you hope it leads to?"
Share back: "Honestly, I picked mine for my parents. Still figuring out if I like it."
example.spot: One step deeper: "Why did you pick it?"
example.feedback: Part 2 asks for a reason, not a fact. Part 4 matters too: sharing your own answer keeps it two-way.

guided.stem: Priya and her new PG roommate have done the "where are you from" round. What is a good next step?
guided.hint: Ask for something meaningful without asking for private facts.

options.text: "What's one thing you're looking forward to this year?"
options.feedback: It is personal but easy to answer, one step deeper.

options.text: Stick to the weather. New people find personal stuff boring.
options.feedback: In the studies, partners cared more than people expected.

options.text: "What does your family earn?"
options.feedback: That asks for a private fact about their family. Deep questions are about what matters to them.

steps.takeaway: Ask one meaningful question and share your answer too.

steps.title: Stay with their last point

hook.stem: What turns a new question into a follow-up?

options.text: It builds on the last point.
options.feedback: It asks for more about what came up.

options.text: It brings in a new topic.
options.feedback: That is a topic switch, not a follow-up.

steps.teach: A follow-up stays with their last point and asks for more, so it shows you heard them and you care. That is how it worked in the studies.

example.ask: Tap the line that asks for more.
parts: A classmate tells you about a new club.
You ask what drew them to it.
You talk about a film you saw.
example.spot: You ask what drew them to it.
example.feedback: This asks about the club they just mentioned, so it is a follow-up. The film line switches topic.

guided.stem: A classmate talks about a club. Which reply keeps that thread alive?

options.text: What drew you to it?
options.feedback: That asks for more about the club.

options.text: Did you see the new film last week?
options.feedback: That line starts a new topic.

steps.takeaway: Ask for more on the same thread.

items.stem: Meera talks about the busy week at her family shop. Which reply breaks that thread?

options.text: Ask what made it so busy.
options.feedback: That stays with her shop news and lets her add more.

options.text: Jump to the exam date.
options.feedback: A new exam topic cuts off the chat about her shop.

options.text: Ask which part of the week felt most busy.
options.feedback: This asks for more on the same week she brought up.

items.stem: A hostel classmate mentions a cricket match. You want to show interest. What fits?

options.text: Ask what stood out, then share your own match story.
options.feedback: The question stays with their match. Your story can come after.

options.text: Tell your own match story first, then keep on talking about it.
options.feedback: That is your story, not a question about theirs.

options.text: Ask about tomorrow's exam instead.
options.feedback: An exam question starts a new topic. It does not follow up.

items.stem: Which wrong guess made people fear that deep talk would feel odd?

options.text: They expected less care.
options.feedback: They thought the other person would care less than they really did.

options.text: The talk really was awkward.
options.feedback: Partners cared more than people expected in the studies.

options.text: The questions were about private facts.
options.feedback: Deep talk in the study meant personal and meaningful talk.

items.stem: A new college roommate answers where she is from. Which next question goes one step deeper?

options.text: What are you looking forward to here?
options.feedback: It asks what she hopes for, but does not pry.

options.text: What does your family earn?
options.feedback: That asks for a private fact. Deep questions are about what matters to her.

options.text: Do not ask. New people dislike personal questions.
options.feedback: In the studies, people expected less care than partners showed.

items.stem: In the coded chats, about what share of all questions were follow-ups?

options.text: About 40%.
options.feedback: Follow-ups were the most common type, 40.51% of questions.

options.text: About 5%.
options.feedback: Too low. Follow-ups were the most common type.

items.stem: A classmate talks about her first day at college. Fill the next step: hear her point, then ___.

options.text: Ask for more.
options.feedback: A follow-up asks her to say more about her point.

options.text: Move at once to a new topic that you had set up.
options.feedback: That switches to a new topic, so her point gets dropped instead of followed up.

concepts.title: Listening
concepts.hook: How can you show that you heard someone, and help a new name stick?
concepts.askLine: When a friend tells you about a hard day, what could you say before offering ideas?
concepts.rule: Say back the gist, ask about it, and stay engaged. For a new name, try to recall it before you check. Name games in classes found recall works.

claims.text: Active listening, as one study defines it, has three parts: say back the gist in your own words, ask when it fits, and stay engaged with your face and body.
In one study of first meetings, active listening made people feel more understood than advice or short replies like 'I see'.
But it did not beat advice on satisfaction or liking; effects were small.
A paraphrase alone did not make people feel understood in an earlier study.
In five tests, listening with care and without judging made speakers feel less anxious while they talked.
In classes, a name game built on recall beat pairwise introductions at 30 minutes, 2 weeks and 11 months.
The gain came from recalling, not from hearing names more often.
A short refresher after 2 weeks helped further.

misconceptions.name: Advice is the best way to show I care.
misconceptions.correction: Advice is not wrong, but in the study it did not make people feel as understood.

misconceptions.name: Repeating is the same as recalling.
misconceptions.correction: When repeats were matched, recalling still won.

sources.title: Weger et al. (2014), study of active listening
Weger, Castle and Emmett (2010), study of paraphrasing
Itzchakov et al. (2018), study of listening
Morris and Fritz (2000), name game study
Morris and Fritz (2002), name game follow-up

quest.title: Listen and recall
quest.detail: Say back what one person told you, in your own words. Later, recall one new name before you check.

steps.title: Show you are listening

hook.stem: In one study of first meetings, which reply made people feel most understood?

options.text: Quick advice on how to prepare next time.
options.feedback: In one study, active listening helped more with feeling understood.

options.text: Say back what you heard, then ask about it.
options.feedback: This uses more of the active listening package.

options.text: "I see."
options.feedback: Short replies like 'I see' left people feeling the least understood in that study.

steps.teach: People felt more understood when a listener gave back the gist and asked about it, so try both. Advice and 'I see' did less.

right.title: Active listening
lines: So round one didn't go your way.
How are you feeling about round two?

example.ask: Tap the line that says it back.
parts: Sana: "My manager redid my whole deck and didn't tell me."
Rohan closes his laptop and turns to her.
Rohan: "So he changed your work without a word to you."
Rohan: "What bugged you more, the changes or not being told?"
Rohan: "Want ideas, or did you just need to vent?"
example.spot: Rohan: "So he changed your work without a word to you."
example.feedback: Part 3 says the gist back in Rohan's words. Part 4 asks about it. Part 5 asks before giving advice, which the study did not test but fits the idea.

guided.stem: At a family function, Tanvi tells her cousin: "I didn't get placed in the first round." Which reply fits active listening best?
guided.hint: Say back the gist, then ask.

options.text: "Apply off-campus. That's what worked for me."
options.feedback: Advice is not wrong, but in the study it did not make people feel as understood.

options.text: "So round one didn't go your way. How are you feeling about round two?"
options.feedback: It says the gist back and asks about it.

options.text: "Hmm."
options.feedback: Short replies like 'I see' or 'OK' left people feeling the least understood in that study.

steps.takeaway: Say back the gist, ask, and stay with them.

steps.title: Keep a new name

hook.stem: New hostel wing, 10 names in 10 minutes. Which helped more in name studies?

options.text: Hearing each name many times.
options.feedback: Recall beat a task with the same number of repeats.

options.text: Trying to recall the names yourself, a little later.
options.feedback: The name game studies point to recall practice.

options.text: Being introduced once, in pairs.
options.feedback: Pairwise introductions did worse than the name game at 30 minutes, 2 weeks and 11 months.

steps.teach: Try to pull a new name from memory before you check it, since recalling beat hearing it the same number of times in class name games.

left.title: Hear it again
lines: Look at the group list first.

example.ask: Tap where he recalls names before the list.
parts: Orientation day. "Hi, I'm Farhan."
"Farhan, which floor are you on?"
At lunch, before checking the group list: "Farhan, Neha, Vikram..."
Next morning: "Hi Farhan!"
example.spot: At lunch, before checking the group list: "Farhan, Neha, Vikram..."
example.feedback: Part 3 recalls the names with no help. In the name game studies, that kind of recall is what helped.

guided.stem: Aditi joins a club meet with 8 new people. Which plan fits what the studies found?
guided.hint: Try to retrieve the names before looking.

options.text: Repeat each name in her head ten times right away.
options.feedback: When repeats were matched, recalling still won.

options.text: After the meet, try to recall all 8, then check the list.
options.feedback: Recall first, then check. That is retrieval practice.

options.text: Skip it. Names stick if you care enough.
options.feedback: The studies did not test caring. They found that practising recall helped.

steps.takeaway: Try to recall a name before checking it.

steps.title: Use the full set

hook.stem: Is saying it back, on its own, the whole of active listening?

options.text: No. Ask and stay with them too.
options.feedback: The full set has more than an echo.

options.text: Yes. One short echo does the full job on its own.
options.feedback: In one study, a paraphrase alone did not make people feel understood.

steps.teach: Saying it back is one part. Alone, it did not help much in one study, so add a question about it and stay engaged.

example.ask: Tap the part that adds to saying it back.
parts: A friend tells you a plan fell through.
You say the plan fell through.
You ask what part felt worst.
example.spot: You ask what part felt worst.
example.feedback: Part 2 only says it back. Part 3 adds a question, which is the next part of active listening.

guided.stem: A friend tells you her train was late. What adds to saying it back?
guided.hint: Saying it back is just one move.

options.text: Ask how it felt.
options.feedback: A question is the second part of active listening.

options.text: Give her tips for next time.
options.feedback: That is advice. In the study, advice made people feel less understood than active listening.

steps.takeaway: Saying it back is one part. Add a question.

items.stem: Which reply leaves out the main parts of active listening?

options.text: Say back the gist, ask, and stay.
options.feedback: That uses all three parts: say back the gist, ask, and stay with them.

options.text: Say hmm, then look away.
options.feedback: A small sound with no care or question leaves out the full set.

options.text: Give tips straight away.
options.feedback: Advice is a different move. The study compared it with active listening.

items.stem: In the college canteen, a friend says their viva went badly. Which reply fits the full package?

options.text: So the viva didn't go how you hoped. Which part felt hardest?
options.feedback: It says back the gist and invites the friend to say more.

options.text: Use my notes next time. They worked for me.
options.feedback: That is advice. In the study, advice made people feel less understood than active listening.

options.text: Your viva went badly.
options.feedback: A paraphrase alone did not make people feel understood in an earlier study.

items.stem: Why try to recall a new club member's name before looking at the list?

options.text: Recall practice helped more than matched repeats.
options.feedback: The name games still won when time and repeats were matched.

options.text: Repeating and recalling are the same.
options.feedback: Hearing it again is not as good as trying to recall it.

options.text: Checking a list first makes the name easier to retrieve.
options.feedback: Looking first removes the chance to try recalling it yourself.

items.stem: After college orientation, Aditi wants to recall eight names. What could she try?

options.text: Recall the eight names, check the list, then try again later.
options.feedback: This uses recall practice and a later refresher.

options.text: Read the list eight times without testing herself.
options.feedback: Matched repeats did not work as well as recall in the study.

options.text: Wait for the names to return on their own.
options.feedback: The studies found a benefit from practising recall.

items.stem: In the listening study, how many kinds of reply did the team compare?

options.text: About 3.
options.feedback: Active listening, advice, and short replies like 'I see'.

options.text: About 6.
options.feedback: The study compared three: active listening, advice and short replies.

items.stem: Put the two active listening moves in the order the study's listeners used them.

options.text: Say back the gist.
options.feedback: A short gist can show what you heard so far.

options.text: Ask them to say more.
options.feedback: Then ask them to say more, so they can go on with their point.

concepts.title: Chats and disagreements
concepts.hook: How can you keep your view in a disagreement and leave a chat clearly?
concepts.askLine: How could you leave a long chat when neither person has said they want to stop?
concepts.rule: In a disagreement, show you heard the other view, then state yours with care. When leaving, a warm line and a clear goodbye may help. That part was not tested.

claims.text: Receptiveness is a way of talking, and it can be measured.
The recipe: say what you want, not just what is wrong; say you understand; find points you agree on; and soften claims with words like 'I think'.
People using it were seen as better partners and were more persuasive.
On Wikipedia talk pages, people whose posts were more open got fewer rude attacks later.
Chats rarely end when either person wants.
People had little idea when their partner wanted to stop.
Among strangers (Study 2), in almost half of chats both wanted to stop sooner.
After chats, people underrate how much they were liked, including first-year students and their hostel-mates.

misconceptions.name: Blunt is more convincing.
misconceptions.correction: In one study, people who disagreed rated receptive replies as more persuasive, not less.

misconceptions.name: Kind means giving in.
misconceptions.correction: Receptive is not the same as agreeing. You can keep your view.

misconceptions.name: I can tell they want to keep going.
misconceptions.correction: People had little idea when partners wanted to stop. Often both wanted to stop sooner.

sources.title: Yeomans et al. (2020), study of conversational receptiveness
sources.publisher: Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes

sources.title: Mastroianni et al. (2021), study of when conversations end
sources.publisher: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

sources.title: Boothby et al. (2018), study of the liking gap

quest.title: Speak and leave
quest.detail: If a disagreement comes up today, start by showing you heard the other view. End one chat on purpose with a warm line and a goodbye.

steps.title: Disagree kindly

hook.stem: In an argument, does sounding open make you less convincing?

options.text: Yes, it looks weak.
options.feedback: In one study, receptive replies were seen as more persuasive.

options.text: No. In one study, opponents rated open replies as more persuasive.
options.feedback: The writers kept their view while sounding open.

options.text: It makes no difference.
options.feedback: The study found a difference in how persuasive replies seemed.

steps.teach: Show you heard their view and name a point you share, so the talk stays open. Soften with 'I think', and say what you want.

right.title: Receptive reply
lines: I see why it feels safe.
I think design can do that too.

example.ask: Rohan and Neha disagree. Tap the common ground.
parts: "I get it, splitting by topic means everyone owns a part."
"And we both want it done before Friday."
"I think the slides might look uneven, though."
"What if we split by topic and one person does a final design pass?"
example.spot: "And we both want it done before Friday."
example.feedback: Part 2 finds a shared goal. Neha still disagrees, and says so with care.

guided.stem: At a family function, an uncle says: "Engineering is the only safe career." Kunal studies design. Which reply is receptive and still keeps Kunal's view?
guided.hint: Acknowledge the concern and keep your view. The study used written replies on US policy topics. Talks with elders were not tested.

options.text: "That's just not true, Uncle. That's outdated."
options.feedback: Words like 'not true' were common in replies rated less receptive.

options.text: "I see why it feels safe, Uncle. We both want me to have a steady job. I think design can do that too. Can I show you where my seniors got placed?"
options.feedback: It acknowledges, agrees, softens, and offers something positive.

options.text: "Okay, Uncle." (and says no more)
options.feedback: Receptive is not the same as agreeing. Kunal can keep his view.

steps.takeaway: Show you heard them, then state your view with care.

steps.title: End a chat well

hook.stem: In a US lab study of chats between strangers, how often did both people want it to end sooner than it did?

options.text: Hardly ever.
options.feedback: In the study, this happened much more often.

options.text: About 1 in 10.
options.feedback: The share was closer to half. About 1 in 10 is how often both wanted it to go on longer.

options.text: Almost half the time.
options.feedback: In Study 2, both wanted an earlier end in 46.83% of chats.

steps.teach: We often can't tell when the other person wants to stop, so a warm, clear goodbye is fine. They may want to go too. Goodbye lines were not tested.

left.title: Hide it
lines: Keep talking and hope they end it.

parts: "I've got to call home before 10."
"Loved hearing about your trek."
"Canteen tomorrow?"
"See you, Meera!"
example.feedback: Part 4 ends it clearly. Part 2 adds a warm line first. Using her name ties back to the names step.

guided.stem: At a college fest stall, Vikram has talked with a senior for 25 minutes. He wants to go. What fits what the studies found?
guided.hint: People are poor at reading when a partner wants to stop.

options.text: Stay until the senior ends it. Leaving first is rude.
options.feedback: People had little idea when partners wanted to stop. Often both wanted to stop sooner.

options.text: Say a warm line and a clear goodbye.
options.feedback: The senior may want to stop too. A clear exit was not tested, but it gives both of you the missing information.

options.text: Keep checking his phone until the senior gets the hint.
options.feedback: In the study, people mostly kept their wish to stop to themselves, so partners had little to go on.

steps.takeaway: A warm line and a clear goodbye can help end a chat.

steps.title: The chat may run long

hook.stem: Do both people in a chat ever want it to end sooner?

options.text: Yes, this can happen a lot.
options.feedback: Many pairs had that same wish.

options.text: No, both people tend to want the chat to last a lot more time.
options.feedback: Only about 1 in 10 pairs both wanted it longer.

steps.teach: In nearly half of the stranger chats in one US study, both people wished to stop sooner. We may miss that wish, so a clear end is fine.

parts: At a college fest, two people talk by a stall.
One says the chat was fun.
One says goodbye and walks on.
example.spot: One says goodbye and walks on.
example.feedback: Part 3 ends the chat clearly. Part 2 is a warm line before it.

guided.stem: At a college event, a chat has run long. What ends it in a clear way?
guided.hint: Look for a line that closes the chat.

options.text: Good to see you. Bye!
options.feedback: The line is warm and has a clear end.

options.text: Keep talking until they say they have to go.
options.feedback: They may be waiting for you. In the study, both often wanted to stop sooner.

steps.takeaway: A warm, clear end is fine. They may want to go too.

items.stem: Which line sounds least open when two college mates disagree?

options.text: I think we could try a new way.
options.feedback: 'I think' is a hedge, part of the recipe.

options.text: Your plan is wrong.
options.feedback: 'Wrong' is a negation. Negations were common in replies rated less receptive.

options.text: I see your point, and I think another way could work.
options.feedback: That says you see their point and softens yours with 'I think'.

items.stem: In a college group project, Neha dislikes the slide plan. Which reply keeps her view?

options.text: I see why that split helps. We both want a clear deck. I think one design pass could help.
options.feedback: It shows understanding, finds common ground, and states a different view.

options.text: No. Your plan is wrong.
options.feedback: Plain negation was rated less receptive in the study.

options.text: Fine. We will do it your way.
options.feedback: She can sound open and still keep her own view.

items.stem: In a college canteen, two new people keep chatting. Can each tell when the other wants to stop?

options.text: They have little idea.
options.feedback: That is what the study found about partners' wishes.

options.text: They can usually tell.
options.feedback: People had little idea when their partners wanted to end.

options.text: Their wishes line up on each chat.
options.feedback: The study found that partners' wishes often did not match.

items.stem: A college fest chat runs long. Which account stays closest to the evidence?

options.text: Partners often misread when to stop; a warm exit is a suggested way to be clear.
options.feedback: The mismatch was studied. The warm exit is an inference, not a tested line.

options.text: A warm exit line was proven to make each chat end well.
options.feedback: No study here tested exit lines, so 'proven' goes too far.

options.text: If the other person is smiling, you know they want to keep going.
options.feedback: People had little idea when partners wanted to stop.

items.stem: In one US lab study of stranger chats, about what share had both people wish to end sooner?

options.text: About 47%.
options.feedback: That is close to half of the stranger chats in the study.

options.text: About 5%, or just a few of the chats in the study.
options.feedback: That is too low; close to half of the pairs wished to stop sooner.

items.stem: A college chat has gone on for a while. Which line sums up the finding?

options.text: We may miss their wish to stop.
options.feedback: People had little sense of when the other person wished to end.

options.text: The other person can read each small hint and will stop right on time.
options.feedback: People were poor at gauging when a chat partner wished to stop.

concepts.title: Reach out
concepts.hook: When might it help to ask someone for advice or send a short check-in?
concepts.askLine: Who could you ask about a hard task, and what would you say you have tried?
concepts.rule: Ask someone with expertise about a hard task. A short personal check-in may be valued more than you expect.

claims.text: People avoid asking for advice for fear of looking incompetent, and the fear is misplaced.
Advice-seekers are seen as more competent.
The boost was bigger when the task was hard, when the adviser was an expert, and when the person judging was the one being asked.
People underrate how much others value a short check-in or small gesture.
The gap is bigger with people you are less close to, and when it is a surprise.
In a crisis, a person is less apt to help when more people are near.
But this is weaker when the others are people you know.
In one US campus study, students sent a check-in note to a classmate. On a 1 to 7 scale, senders guessed about 5.6. The classmates gave about 6.2.

misconceptions.name: The effect works for any question.
misconceptions.correction: On easy tasks, asking gave no boost, but it did no harm either.

misconceptions.name: Asking means I'm weak.
misconceptions.correction: The study found this fear was misplaced.

misconceptions.name: Distance makes it unwelcome.
misconceptions.correction: Less-close people still valued it, and senders underrated them even more.

sources.title: Brooks, Gino and Schweitzer (2015), study of advice seeking
Liu et al. (2023), study of reaching out
sources.publisher: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

sources.title: Fischer et al. (2011), bystander effect review

quest.title: Ask and check in
quest.detail: Ask one experienced person about a hard task. In the daytime, send one short check-in to someone you haven't talked to in a while. Then close the app.

steps.title: Ask a senior for advice

hook.stem: At your internship you are stuck on a hard task. Does asking your senior for advice make you look less capable?

options.text: Yes, it shows you can't cope.
options.feedback: In the studies, this fear was misplaced.

options.text: No. In studies, people who asked for advice on hard tasks were seen as more competent.
options.feedback: The effect was strongest for hard tasks and expert advisers. These were lab and online studies, not offices.
